title: III. The Brothers Make Friends
paragraphs: Ivan, though, wasn't in a separate room, only behind a screen that kept him hidden from the rest of the room. It was the first room off the entrance, with a buffet counter along the wall. Waiters kept darting back and forth through it. The only other customer in the room was an old retired army man drinking tea in a corner. But there was the usual racket coming from the other rooms of the tavern—shouts for waiters, the pop of corks, the click of billiard balls, the drone of a barrel organ. Alyosha knew Ivan didn't usually come to this tavern and disliked taverns in general. So he must have come here, Alyosha reasoned, simply to meet Dmitri by arrangement. And yet Dmitri wasn't there.
"Shall I order you fish, soup, something? You can't live on tea alone, I suppose," Ivan cried, clearly delighted to have caught hold of Alyosha. He'd finished his dinner and was drinking tea.
"Let me have soup, and tea after, I'm hungry," Alyosha said cheerfully.
"And cherry jam? They have it here. Remember how you used to love cherry jam when you were little?"
"You remember that? Let me have jam too, I still like it."
Ivan rang for the waiter and ordered soup, jam, and tea.

"I remember everything, Alyosha, I remember you up until you were eleven—I was nearly fifteen. There's such a gap between fifteen and eleven that brothers are never really companions at those ages. I don't even know if I was fond of you back then. When I first went off to Moscow, I never thought about you at all for the first few years. Then, when you came to Moscow yourself, I believe we only met once, somewhere. And now I've been here more than three months, and so far we've barely said two words to each other. I'm leaving tomorrow, and I was just sitting here thinking how I might see you to say goodbye, and just then you walked by."
"Were you so anxious to see me, then?"

"Very. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. And then say goodbye. I think it's always best to get to know people right before you part from them. I've noticed how you've been looking at me these past three months. There's been a constant look of expectation in your eyes, and I can't stand that. That's why I've kept my distance from you. But in the end I've come to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. Though I'm laughing as I say it, I mean it seriously. You really do stand firm, don't you? I like people who hold firm to something, whatever it is, even when they're as small as you are. Your expectant eyes stopped annoying me—I grew fond of them, eventually, those expectant eyes of yours. You seem to love me, for some reason, Alyosha?"

"I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you—Ivan is a grave. I say of you—Ivan is a riddle. You're still a riddle to me, even now. But I understand something about you, something I didn't understand until this morning."
"What's that?" Ivan laughed.
"You won't be angry?" Alyosha laughed too.
"Well?"
"That you're every bit as young as other young men of twenty-three, that you're simply a young, fresh, decent boy, green, in fact! Now, have I insulted you terribly?"

"On the contrary, I'm struck by a coincidence," Ivan cried, warmly and good-naturedly. "Would you believe it, ever since that scene with her, I've thought of nothing but my own youthful greenness, and here you are, as if you'd guessed it, bringing it up yourself. Do you know, I've been sitting here thinking to myself: even if I stopped believing in life, if I lost faith in the woman I love, lost faith in the order of things, became convinced, in fact, that everything is a disorderly, damnable, maybe even devil-ridden chaos, even if I were struck by every horror of human disillusionment—I'd still want to live, and having once put the cup to my lips, I wouldn't turn away from it until I'd drained it dry! At thirty, though, I'll surely set the cup down, even unfinished, and turn away—to where, I don't know. But until I'm thirty, I know my youth will win out over everything—every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I've asked myself many times whether there's any despair in the world that could overpower this frantic, maybe unseemly thirst for life in me, and I've concluded there isn't—not until I'm thirty, anyway, and then I imagine I'll lose it on my own. Some sniveling, consumptive moralists—poets especially—often call that thirst for life base. It's a Karamazov trait, true enough, that thirst for life regardless of everything; you probably have it too, no doubt, but why call it base? The centripetal force on this planet of ours is still terribly strong, Alyosha. I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. Even if I don't believe in the order of the universe, I still love the sticky little leaves as they unfurl in spring. I love the blue sky, I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, even though I may have long since stopped believing in them, my heart still prizes them out of old habit. Here, they've brought your soup, eat it, it'll do you good. It's excellent soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel through Europe, Alyosha, I'll set off from here. And yet I know I'm only going to a graveyard, but it's a most precious graveyard, that's the thing! Precious are the dead who lie there, every stone over them speaks of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I'll fall to the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them—even though in my heart I'm convinced it's long since become nothing but a graveyard. And I won't weep out of despair, but simply because I'll be happy in my tears, I'll steep my soul in that emotion. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that's really all it is. It's not a matter of intellect or logic, it's loving with one's insides, with one's gut. One loves the first raw strength of one's youth. Do you understand any of this rant of mine, Alyosha?" Ivan suddenly laughed.

"I understand it all too well, Ivan. One longs to love with one's insides, with one's gut. You put that beautifully, and I'm so glad you have such a longing for life," Alyosha cried. "I think everyone ought to love life above everything else in the world."
"Love life more than its meaning?"

"Absolutely—love it regardless of logic, as you say, it has to be regardless of logic, and only then will one understand its meaning. I've thought that for a long time. Half your work is already done, Ivan, you love life—now you just have to try for the second half, and you'll be saved."
"You're trying to save me, but maybe I'm not lost at all! And what does this second half of yours mean?"
"Why, one has to raise up your dead, who perhaps haven't died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I'm so glad of this talk, Ivan."
"I can see you're feeling inspired. I'm awfully fond of these professions of faith from—novices, like you. You're a steadfast sort, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?"
"Yes, my elder is sending me out into the world."

"Then we'll see each other out there, in the world. We'll meet again before I turn thirty, when I'll start turning away from the cup. Father doesn't want to turn away from his cup until he's seventy—he dreams of hanging on until eighty, in fact, or so he says. He means it far too seriously, buffoon though he is. He too stands on solid rock—he stands on his own sensuality—though once we're past thirty, there may genuinely be nothing else left to stand on.... But hanging on until seventy is disgusting; better to stop at thirty; one might still keep 'a shadow of nobility' by deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?"
"No, but I saw Smerdyakov," and Alyosha quickly, though in careful detail, described his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan started listening anxiously and began questioning him.
"But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he'd told me about him," Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and fell into thought.
"Are you frowning on Smerdyakov's account?" Alyosha asked.
"Yes, on his account. Damn him, I did want to see Dmitri, but there's no need now," Ivan said reluctantly.
"But are you really leaving so soon, brother?"
"Yes."
"What about Dmitri and father—how will it all end?" Alyosha asked anxiously.

"You keep harping on that! What business is it of mine? Am I my brother Dmitri's keeper?" Ivan snapped irritably, then suddenly smiled bitterly. "That's Cain's answer about his murdered brother, isn't it? Maybe that's what you're thinking right now? Well, damn it all, I can't stay here to be their keeper, can I? I've finished what I came to do, and I'm leaving. Do you imagine I'm jealous of Dmitri, that I've been trying to steal his lovely Katerina Ivanovna for the last three months? Nonsense, I had business of my own to settle. I've finished it. I'm leaving. I finished it just now—you were there to see it."
"At Katerina Ivanovna's?"

"Yes, and I've freed myself once and for all. And really, what business is it of mine, Dmitri's? Dmitri doesn't even come into it. I had my own affairs to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know perfectly well, on the other hand, that Dmitri behaved as though there were some understanding between us. I never asked him to do that, but he solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It's all too absurd. Ah, Alyosha, if only you knew how light my heart feels now! Would you believe it, I sat here eating my dinner and nearly ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Pah! It went on for nearly six months, and all at once I've thrown it off. I couldn't have guessed, even yesterday, how easy it would be to put an end to it, once I actually wanted to."
"You're talking about your love, Ivan?"

"My love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady, fretted over her, and she fretted over me. I sat there keeping watch over her... and then all at once it collapsed! I spoke with real inspiration this morning, but once I left I burst out laughing. Would you believe it? Yes, it's the literal truth."
"You seem quite merry about it now," Alyosha observed, studying his face, which had suddenly brightened.

"But how was I supposed to know I didn't care for her in the least! Ha ha! Turns out I didn't, after all. And yet how she drew me in! How attractive she was, just now, while I was making my little speech! And you know, she still draws me in terribly, even now, and yet how easy it is to walk away from her. You think I'm bragging?"
"No, maybe it just wasn't love."

"Alyosha," Ivan laughed, "don't go philosophizing about love, it doesn't suit you. How you threw yourself into that discussion this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was like sitting beside a 'laceration.' Ah, she knew perfectly well how much I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri," Ivan insisted cheerfully. "Her feeling for Dmitri was pure self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was absolutely true, but the worst of it is, it might take her fifteen or twenty years to realize she doesn't care for Dmitri at all, and loves me instead, the one she torments, and maybe she'll never realize it, despite today's lesson. Well, it's better this way; I can simply walk away for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I left?"
Alyosha told him she'd had hysterics, and that now, from what he'd heard, she was unconscious and delirious.
"Isn't Madame Hohlakov exaggerating?"
"I don't think so."
"I ought to find out. But no one dies from hysterics, anyway. They don't matter. God gave women hysterics as a kind of relief. I won't go see her at all. Why push myself forward again?"
"But you told her she'd never cared for you."
"I did that on purpose. Alyosha, shall I order some champagne? Let's drink to my freedom. Ah, if only you knew how glad I am!"
"No, brother, better not drink," Alyosha said suddenly. "Besides, I feel somehow low."
"Yes, you've been low for a while, I've noticed it."
"So you've decided to leave tomorrow morning, then?"

"Morning? I never said I'd leave in the morning.... But maybe it will be the morning. Would you believe it, I only dined here today to avoid dining with the old man, I loathe him so much. As far as he's concerned, I should have left long ago. But why are you so worried about my leaving? We've got plenty of time before I go—an eternity!"
"If you're leaving tomorrow, what do you mean by an eternity?"

"But what does it matter to us?" Ivan laughed. "We've got time enough for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Answer me: why did we meet here? To talk about my love for Katerina Ivanovna, about the old man and Dmitri? About foreign travel? About the fatal state of Russia? About the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?"
"No."

"Then you know why. It's different for other people, but we, in our green youth, have to settle the eternal questions first of all. That's what matters to us. Young Russia does nothing but talk about the eternal questions these days. Just when the older generation has thrown itself into practical concerns. Why have you been looking at me with that expectant look for the last three months? To ask me, 'What do you believe, or don't you believe at all?' Isn't that what your eyes have been asking, these three months?"
"Perhaps so," Alyosha smiled. "You're not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?"

"Me, laughing! I don't want to wound my little brother, who's been watching me with such expectation for three months. Alyosha, look straight at me! Of course, I'm just as much a little boy as you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been up to, up until now—some of them, anyway? Take this reeking tavern, for instance—they meet here and sit down in a corner. They've never met once in their lives before, and once they leave the tavern, they won't meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about, in that brief pause in the tavern? The eternal questions—whether God exists, whether there's immortality. And the ones who don't believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism instead, about remaking the whole of humanity on some new pattern—which amounts to the same thing, really, the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn't that so?"

"Yes, for real Russians, the question of whether God exists, and of immortality—or, as you put it, the same questions turned inside out—comes first and foremost, of course, and it should," said Alyosha, still watching his brother with that same gentle, questioning smile.

"Well, Alyosha, sometimes it's very unwise to be Russian at all, but it's hard to imagine anything stupider than the way Russian boys spend their time. Still, there's one Russian boy named Alyosha I'm awfully fond of."
"How nicely you put that!" Alyosha suddenly laughed.
"Well, tell me where to start, give the orders. The existence of God, eh?"
"Start wherever you like. You announced yesterday, at father's, that there's no God." Alyosha looked searchingly at his brother.

"I said that yesterday at dinner on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes light up. But I've got no objection to discussing it with you now, and I say that quite seriously. I want us to be friends, Alyosha, because I have no friends, and I want to try having one. Well, just imagine, maybe I accept God too," Ivan laughed; "that's a surprise for you, isn't it?"
"Yes, of course, if you're not joking now."

"Joking? I was told at the elder's yesterday that I was joking. You know, dear boy, there was an old sinner back in the eighteenth century who declared that if God didn't exist, He'd have to be invented. _S'il n'existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l'inventer._ And man has, in fact, invented God. And what's strange, what would truly be marvelous, isn't that God should actually exist—the marvel is that such an idea, the idea of the necessity of God, could ever occur to such a savage, vicious beast as man. So holy is it, so moving, so wise, and such credit does it do to mankind. As for me, I made up my mind long ago not to trouble over whether man created God or God created man. And I won't run through all the axioms Russian boys lay down on that subject, all borrowed from European hypotheses—because what's a hypothesis there is treated as an axiom by the Russian boy, and not only by the boys but by their teachers too, since our Russian professors are often just the same boys themselves, grown up. So I'll skip all the hypotheses. What are we actually driving at here? I'm trying to explain, as quickly as I can, my essential nature—what sort of man I am, what I believe, what I hope for—that's it, isn't it? And so I tell you, I accept God, plainly and simply. But note this: if God exists, and if He really did create the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to Euclidean geometry, and the human mind with the concept of only three dimensions in space. And yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers—some of them among the most distinguished—who wonder whether the whole universe, or more broadly speaking, the whole of existence, was really created only according to Euclid's geometry; they even dare to imagine that two parallel lines, which by Euclid's rules can never meet on earth, might meet somewhere out in infinity. I've come to the conclusion that since I can't even understand that much, I certainly can't expect to understand anything about God. I admit humbly that I lack the capacity to settle such questions; I have a Euclidean, earthly mind, so how could I possibly solve problems that don't belong to this world at all? And my advice to you is never to think about it either, my dear Alyosha, especially about God, about whether He exists or not. All such questions are simply unsuited to a mind built around only three dimensions. And so I accept God, and gladly, and what's more, I accept His wisdom, His purpose, which lie utterly beyond our grasp; I believe in some underlying order, some meaning to life; I believe in the eternal harmony they say we'll all be blended into one day. I believe in the Word toward which the universe is striving, the Word that was itself 'with God,' and that is itself God, and so on, and so on, into infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right track, don't I? And yet, would you believe it, in the end I don't accept this world of God's—and even though I know it exists, I don't accept it at all. It's not that I reject God, you understand, it's the world He created that I don't, and can't, accept. Let me put it plainly. I believe, like a child, that suffering will be healed, made up for, that all the humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like some pitiful mirage, like the wretched invention of man's feeble, infinitely small Euclidean mind, that in the world's final act, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will happen that it will be enough for every heart, enough to soothe every grievance, to atone for every crime humanity has ever committed, for all the blood they've spilled; that it will make it possible not merely to forgive but to justify everything that has ever happened to men—but even if all that comes to pass, I still don't accept it. I won't accept it. Even if the parallel lines meet and I see it with my own eyes, I'll see it and say they've met, but I still won't accept it. That's what lies at the root of me, Alyosha; that's my creed. I'm entirely serious about what I'm saying. I began our conversation as stupidly as I possibly could, on purpose, but it's led straight to my confession, because that's really all you wanted. You didn't want to hear about God—you wanted to know what the brother you love actually lives by. And now I've told you."
Ivan wrapped up his long tirade with a striking, unexpected show of feeling.
"And why did you begin 'as stupidly as you could'?" Alyosha asked, gazing dreamily at him.

"For one thing, for the sake of being Russian. Russian conversations on subjects like this are always carried on with unbelievable stupidity. And second, the more stupid one is, the closer one gets to reality. Stupidity is blunt and artless, while intelligence squirms and hides itself away. Intelligence is a swindler, but stupidity is honest and straightforward. I've steered the conversation toward my own despair, and the more stupidly I've laid it out, the better for me."
"You'll explain why you don't accept the world?" Alyosha said.

"Of course I will, it's no secret, it's exactly what I've been building up to. Dear little brother, I don't want to corrupt you, or shake you loose from your foundation—maybe I want you to heal me instead." Ivan suddenly smiled, quite like a gentle little child. Alyosha had never seen a smile like that on his face before.
